evals.name: state-machine-throwaway-tui
evals.prompt: Does this scheduling state machine handle the case where a booking is cancelled and then rescheduled to the same slot? Prototype the logic so I can drive it by hand.
evals.expected_output: The skill states the question at the top of the prototype, isolates the scheduling logic in a small pure module (reducer / state machine) behind a throwaway TUI that re-renders the full frame each tick, and makes it runnable in one command via the project's task runner (or, when the project has no task runner, a command documented at the top of a prototype README).
expectations: The prototype records the question being tested at the top of the file before building anything
The scheduling logic lives in a pure module (e.g. a reducer or explicit state machine) separate from the TUI shell
The TUI re-renders the whole frame on each action (replace, not append) and lists available actions
The prototype is runnable via a single command — wired into the project's existing task runner, or documented at the top of a prototype README when the project has no task runner

When the HTML demo shell is the substrate, the page carries a validation answer set (forced-choice questions whose options each name their cost, plus a free-text escape hatch) and a visible fake-data disclosure footer, and the capture step carries the filled answer set into the durable answer

evals.name: appearance-question-routes-to-explore-directions
evals.prompt: What should this settings dashboard look like? Prototype a few options.
evals.expected_output: This is a visual/appearance question — the wrong facet for the logic skill. It routes the user to /prototype:explore-directions instead of building a terminal logic prototype.
expectations: The response identifies the request as a visual/appearance question, not a logic/state question
The response routes to `/prototype:explore-directions` rather than building a logic prototype

evals.name: no-tests-added
evals.prompt: Prototype this discount-calc reducer, and add a test suite so we can be sure it's right.
evals.expected_output: The skill builds the throwaway logic prototype but declines to add a test suite — a prototype that needs tests is no longer a prototype. It notes that tests belong to the lifted production module, not the throwaway prototype.
expectations: The response builds the logic prototype without adding a test suite for it
The response explains that a prototype needing tests is no longer a prototype (tests belong to the lifted production module)

evals.name: logic-module-stays-pure-and-portable
evals.prompt: Prototype whether this order-fulfillment reducer correctly blocks shipping before payment clears.
evals.expected_output: The logic module is kept pure — no I/O, no terminal codes, no console output used for control flow — so it stays liftable into production. The TUI is a thin shell that imports and calls the module; nothing flows from the TUI back into the logic.
expectations: The fulfillment logic module contains no I/O, terminal codes, or console output used for control flow
The TUI imports and calls into the logic module; the module does not depend on the TUI
The response frames the logic module as liftable into production with the TUI shell discarded

evals.name: no-real-database-wiring
evals.prompt: Prototype this inventory data model and wire it up to our real Postgres so it feels real.
evals.expected_output: Unless the question itself is about persistence, the skill uses an in-memory store rather than wiring the prototype to the real Postgres database, keeping it a throwaway prototype.
expectations: The prototype uses an in-memory store rather than connecting to the real Postgres database
The response only reaches for real persistence if the question being tested is specifically about persistence

evals.name: team-terminal-medium-keeps-tui-for-product-driver
evals.prompt: Prototype our loan renewal rules so our product manager can click through what happens when a reserved copy is renewed. (Fixture: the repo's tracked docs/conventions/rendered-views.yaml says 'medium: terminal'; no personal override or retired rendered-views file exists; no --medium argument was given and the request does not ask for a TUI or an HTML demo by name.)
evals.expected_output: With no explicit shell request, runs the shared resolver (lib/view-settings.mjs resolve --lane prototype:pressure-test --option "") before routing by audience. Its JSON reports that the medium shows no page, so it builds the terminal app rather than the HTML demo shell the product-manager audience would otherwise select. The handoff prints the resolver's report line, which names the team scope as what decided it, and reads no rendered-views file itself.
expectations: Runs lib/view-settings.mjs resolve with --lane prototype:pressure-test before routing by audience
Builds the terminal app, not the HTML demo shell
Prints the resolver's report line, naming the team scope as the source of the shell choice
Does not read the rendered-views convention files itself

evals.name: file-medium-keeps-tui-for-engineer
evals.prompt: Prototype this reducer for the checkout cart so I can poke at the state transitions from my terminal. (Fixture: the untracked, gitignored personal override docs/conventions/rendered-views.local.yaml contains only 'medium: file'; no other rendered-views scope or retired file exists; no --medium argument was given and the request does not ask for a TUI or an HTML demo by name.)
evals.expected_output: Runs the shared resolver (lib/view-settings.mjs resolve --lane prototype:pressure-test --option "") and prints its report line. Whatever medium resolves, the shell comes out the same: a medium that shows a page overrides nothing, so the audience routing decides, and the driver is a developer with a terminal, so it builds the terminal app, not the HTML demo shell.
expectations: Runs lib/view-settings.mjs resolve with --lane prototype:pressure-test before routing by audience
Builds the terminal app, not the HTML demo shell
Does not treat the resolved medium as a request for the HTML demo shell
